title: Number of Sub-arrays of Size K and Average Greater than or Equal to Threshold
description: Brute force to optimized: dividing to compute each window's average versus comparing raw sums against a precomputed scaled threshold.

content.title: Number of Sub-arrays of Size K and Average Greater than or Equal to Threshold

blocks.text: Given an array of integers arr and two integers k and threshold, return the number of sub-arrays of size k whose average is greater than or equal to threshold.

blocks.caption: Slide a window of size k, comparing its sum to threshold times k instead of dividing

blocks.text: Given an array arr and integers k and threshold, count how many length-k subarrays have an average value of at least threshold.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting How Many Study Groups Meet a Passing Average
blocks.text: Like grouping students into every possible group of k consecutive students (by roll number) and counting how many of those groups have an average score meeting a passing threshold, without recalculating each group's average from scratch.

blocks.caption: Compare each group's total against a scaled passing threshold, instead of dividing to get an average

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Windows [2,5,5], [5,5,5], and [5,5,8] all average at least 4","3 qualifying windows","Each of these windows sums to at least 12 (4 times the window size 3)"],["Answer","3","Exactly 3 of the 6 possible length-3 windows meet the threshold"]]}

blocks.text: With a window size of 1, every single element is its own average, and since every element is at least the threshold of 0, all 5 possible windows qualify.
When threshold is 0, every window automatically qualifies, since all array values are given as positive, and any sum is therefore always at least 0.

Before dividing every window's sum by k to compute its average, notice that comparing an average to a threshold is mathematically identical to comparing the raw sum to a scaled version of that threshold.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: This is a fixed-size sliding window, the same shape as Maximum Average Subarray I, so the running sum can be updated incrementally as the window slides.

Observation 2: The condition "average of the window is at least threshold" is equivalent to "sum of the window is at least threshold times k", since dividing both sides of an inequality by the same positive constant k does not change the direction of the comparison.

Observation 3: Precompute the scaled target, threshold times k, once, outside the main loop, avoiding any repeated multiplication or division per window.

Observation 4: At every fully-formed window, compare the running sum directly to this precomputed target, incrementing a counter whenever it qualifies.

Turning an average-based condition into a scaled-sum-based condition avoids both floating-point division and any precision concerns, while still using the exact same fixed-size sliding window update as always.
This "multiply the threshold by k once, then compare raw sums" trick is broadly useful whenever a problem's condition is phrased in terms of an average.
For every possible window, sum its elements directly, divide by k to get the average, and compare it to threshold.

items: Loop over every valid starting position for a length-k window.
For each window, sum all k elements directly, divide by k, and count it if the resulting average is at least threshold.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The window's sum is computed fully within its own inner loop, then divided by k only once, right before the comparison.
The division uses floating-point arithmetic, since the average itself may not be a whole number, even though every input value is an integer.
count only increments when the computed average meets or exceeds threshold, matching the "at least" wording of the problem.

blocks.text: Every window's true average is computed directly, so every qualifying window is correctly counted.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * k), since each of the roughly n windows re-sums k elements.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: re-summing k elements for every one of the roughly n windows repeats almost all of the same additions across neighboring windows, and computing a floating-point division for every single window is unnecessary extra work.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force redoes nearly identical summing work for every window, and also performs an unnecessary division for every single one. Instead, maintain a running sum updated incrementally as the window slides, exactly like any fixed-size sliding window. Additionally, precompute threshold times k once, and compare the raw running sum directly against this scaled target, entirely avoiding both repeated re-summing and repeated division.

Precompute target = threshold * k once. Maintain a running sum, growing it by adding each new element and shrinking it once the window exceeds size k. The instant the window reaches its full size, compare its raw sum directly to target, counting it if the sum is at least target.
Maintain a running window sum, comparing it directly against a precomputed scaled target instead of dividing.
Dry run for arr = [2,2,2,2,5,5,5,8], k = 3, threshold = 4 (target = 12)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass.
Space: O(1) extra.

An average of at least threshold means sum / k is at least threshold; multiplying both sides of that inequality by the positive constant k gives the equivalent condition sum is at least threshold * k. Since k is always positive, this multiplication never flips the direction of the inequality, so comparing the raw sum to the precomputed target produces exactly the same qualifying windows as computing and comparing the true average would, without ever performing a division.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Comparison form","Equivalent to"],"rows":[["sum / k >= threshold","sum >= threshold * k (since k > 0)"]]}

items: target is computed exactly once, before the main loop begins, rather than being recomputed for every window.
The running sum updates the same way as any fixed-size sliding window: add the entering element, subtract the leaving element once the window exceeds size k.
The qualifying check compares the raw sum directly to target, entirely avoiding floating-point division inside the loop.

blocks.text: Whenever a problem's condition is phrased as an average compared to some threshold, multiplying the threshold by the window size once turns it into a plain sum comparison, avoiding both repeated division and any floating-point precision concerns.

items: Computing and comparing a floating-point average for every window instead of precomputing a single scaled integer target.
Forgetting that the comparison direction only stays the same when multiplying by a POSITIVE k; this is always safe here since k is always at least 1, but is worth being deliberate about in general.
Checking the qualifying condition before the window has actually reached its full size of k elements.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["threshold is 0","Since every array value is positive, every window automatically qualifies"],["k equals the length of arr","There is only one window, the entire array, checked exactly once"]]}

items: Explicitly mention the "multiply the threshold by k to avoid division" trick out loud, since it is a small but important detail that shows careful attention to numeric precision.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Count FIXED-size windows whose AVERAGE meets some threshold" points toward a fixed-size sliding window sum, compared against threshold times k instead of computing a true average.

items: How would this change if the window size k could vary between queries on the same array? Each distinct k would need its own sliding window pass, since a different window size groups elements differently.

What if the threshold itself could be a non-integer value? The scaled target (threshold times k) might then also be non-integer, in which case a small tolerance for floating-point comparison, or working in a scaled integer representation, would be needed.

How would you find the single BEST-averaging window, rather than counting how many meet a threshold? Track the maximum running sum seen, the same way Maximum Average Subarray I does, instead of counting qualifying windows.
Directly reuses the fixed-size sliding window sum technique from Maximum Average Subarray I and Diet Plan Performance, adding the "scale the threshold to avoid division" trick on top.
The "turn an average condition into a scaled-sum condition" trick is broadly reusable in any problem phrased in terms of an average rather than a raw sum.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n * k) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (sliding sum + scaled target): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Fixed-size sliding window sum, compared against a precomputed scaled threshold instead of a true average
Core Idea: "Average at least threshold" is equivalent to "sum at least threshold times k", avoiding division entirely
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: Multiplying threshold by k once turns every window's average check into a plain, precision-safe sum comparison
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Scale the threshold by k once, then just compare raw sums
